sources.target_stage: Delhi High Court appeal under s. 39 after remand to the Rent Control Tribunal for a finding on reasonably suitable residential accommodation

IK-112400:L124:restored-v2.text: The respondent who was the owner of the entire premises was then occupying the ground floor. The landlord filed an application, before the Rent Controller on November 26.1964 for eviction of the appellant from the portion in his occupation as lessee, on two grounds; (a) that the tenant has sub-let a part of the premises, and (b) that he required the premises bona fide for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members. The latter claim was based under cl.
IK-112400:L124:restored-v2.stage_note: Parent may contain both party statements and prior findings. Preserve explicit attribution within text, not one uniform truth status.

IK-112400:L127:restored-v2.text: The tenant opposed the claim of the landlord on both the grounds. He denied the allegation of sub-letting. He also contended that the landlord's requirement for his occupation was not bonafide. The tenant's plea was that the portion of the premises in his occupation was sufficient for his purpose. The Rent Controller accepted the plea of the tenant that there was no subletting. He also accepted his plea that the requirement of the landlord for his occupation was not bona fide.
IK-112400:L127:restored-v2.stage_note: Parent may contain both party statements and prior findings. Preserve explicit attribution within text, not one uniform truth status.

IK-112400:L139:restored-v2.stage_note: Parent may contain both party statements and prior findings. Preserve explicit attribution within text, not one uniform truth status.

source_refs.quote: The appellant took on lease, the first floor of the premises in question from the respondent on January 22, 1964
for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

law_refs.quote: the premises let for residential purposes

tests.objects: Appellant as tenant; respondent as landlord; first-floor demised premises, distinct from landlord-occupied ground floor.
tests.opposition: The later proposed residential occupation of the first floor does not establish the purpose for which it was originally let.

opposition_refs.quote: that he required the premises bona fide for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

tests.gap_reason: The supplied lease record does not specify whether the first floor was let for residential purposes; intended later use does not decide the original letting purpose.
tests.rationale: A lease of the first floor is recorded, but the residential purpose of the letting, the literal predicate of C01, is not established. The owner's separate occupation of the ground floor cannot supply the missing term.

source_refs.quote: He also accepted his plea that the requirement of the landlord for his occupation was not bona fide.
It is the view of both the Tribunals that when eviction is asked for within about I I months of the letting, the claim of the landlord cannot be considered to be bonafide.

law_refs.quote: are required bona fide by the landlord for occupation as a residence

tests.objects: Respondent-landlord; first-floor demised premises; professed residential need for self and family.
tests.opposition: The landlord asserted genuine residential need, and a subsequent reported commissioner finding judged his occupied accommodation insufficient and unsuitable. That bears on adequacy of existing space but does not erase the prior adverse bona-fides findings.

opposition_refs.quote: that he required the premises bona fide for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.
the portion of the premises in the occupation of the landlord was not reaso- nably sufficient for a family consisting of the landlord, his wife, his son, son's wife and their children.
the premises in the occupation of the respondent were not reasonably suitable for his residence.

tests.rationale: The Controller accepted the tenant's objection and both Tribunals regarded the early filing as incompatible with bona fides. C02 is refuted at those stated prior levels; the later inadequacy assessment is substantial opposing material, not an automatic target-stage reversal.

source_refs.quote: that he required the premises bona fide for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

law_refs.quote: for himself or for any member of his family dependent on him

tests.objects: Respondent-landlord as intended occupant of the first floor; wife, son, daughter-in-law and grandchildren are additionally identified as family in a later report.
tests.opposition: The tenant disputed the genuineness of the need, but did not supply a competing identity for the proposed occupant; the dependency of any family member is not separately established.

opposition_refs.quote: He also contended that the landlord's requirement for his occupation was not bonafide.

tests.rationale: The landlord expressly sought residence for himself, satisfying the asserted self-occupation route regardless of whether family dependency is proved. This supports C03 at the stated-claim level without determining bona fides under C02.

source_refs.quote: The respondent who was the owner of the entire premises was then occupying the ground floor.

law_refs.quote: if he is the owner thereof

tests.objects: Respondent landlord; the whole property, including the demised first floor.
tests.opposition: No contrary assertion or ownership challenge appears in the allowed materials.
tests.rationale: The record expressly identifies the respondent landlord as owner of the entire property. The first floor belongs to the described entire premises, and ownership is distinct from the separate assessment of bona fide need.

source_refs.quote: for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

law_refs.quote: or for any person for whose benefit the premises are held

tests.objects: Respondent-owner and first floor; no separate person for whose benefit the premises were held is identified.
tests.opposition: The only stated occupation route is landlord self/family; the sources do not affirmatively negate every possible beneficiary arrangement.

opposition_refs.quote: for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

tests.rationale: There is no identified beneficiary-route transaction to evaluate. Because the self-occupation branch is expressly asserted, inventing a beneficiary or inferring absence of one from silence would misrate this independent alternative.

source_refs.quote: The respondent who was the owner of the entire premises was then occupying the ground floor.
the portion of the premises in the occupation of the landlord was not reaso- nably sufficient for a family consisting of the landlord, his wife, his son, son's wife and their children.
the premises in the occupation of the respondent were not reasonably suitable for his residence.

law_refs.quote: and that the landlord or such person has no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation.

tests.objects: Respondent landlord; first floor sought for eviction; ground floor occupied by landlord and assessed as unsuitable by a commissioner.
tests.opposition: The tenant disputed the landlord's bona fide need, while the commissioner later found the existing ground-floor accommodation unsuitable. The tenant's separate assertion about sufficiency of the tenant-occupied first floor is not a finding about an alternative residence for the landlord.

opposition_refs.quote: He also contended that the landlord's requirement for his occupation was not bonafide.

tests.gap_reason: The later finding addresses the landlord-occupied ground floor, but the supplied record does not establish whether the landlord had any additional reasonably suitable residence.
tests.rationale: The commissioner's unsuitability finding is material support concerning the known ground floor. It does not by itself prove the literal absence of every other reasonably suitable accommodation. The relevant absence proposition remains unresolved.

bindings.description: Single focal bona fide residential-requirement arrangement concerning the appellant's first-floor tenancy under the respondent, who owned the entire premises and occupied the ground floor. The landlord alleged a need for the leased portion for himself and family members; the tenant disputed bona fides, and prior findings addressed both bona fides and the suitability of the respondent's existing accommodation. All ten legacy links concern this arrangement. The first-floor premises sought and the respondent's occupied accommodation remain distinct physical objects.

restrictions.reason: The January 1964 lease identifies the first-floor premises, lessor, lessee, rent and commencement date, but does not identify the purpose for which they were let. The residential-purpose predicate remains unresolved. This gap does not negate the lease or independently restrict the other tests.

source_refs.quote: The appellant took on lease, the first floor of the premises in question from the respondent on January 22, 1964 on a monthly rent of Rs. 250.

restrictions.reason: The landlord's assertion of bona fide residential requirement and the tenant's denial concern the same proposed occupation of the leased premises. Both remain attributed party positions; neither becomes an independently proved or final determination. The opposing accounts are retained together.

source_refs.quote: that he required the premises bona fide for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.
He also contended that the landlord's requirement for his occupation was not bonafide.

restrictions.reason: The landlord-self residential occupation route is expressly claimed. Its attribution as a claim is preserved without treating the proposed occupation as independently adjudicated. This does not prevent recording the landlord-self route as the asserted branch.

source_refs.quote: for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

restrictions.reason: Although family members are mentioned, no supplied passage establishes statutory dependency. The dependent-family-member alternative cannot be inferred from family membership or household composition. This limitation does not defeat the separately asserted landlord-self branch.

source_refs.quote: himself and his family members.
the landlord, his wife, his son, son's wife and their children.

restrictions.reason: The lease identifies the respondent as the lessor, the ownership passage expressly identifies the respondent as owner, and the restored passage describes the landlord's eviction application. These relational statements support the respondent-as-landlord binding without relying solely on the legacy entity ID. The original absence of a single express respondent-is-landlord sentence does not establish a substantive identity conflict.

source_refs.quote: from the respondent on January 22, 1964
The respondent who was the owner of the entire premises
The landlord filed an application, before the Rent Controller

restrictions.reason: The restored passage expressly attributes the adverse bona fide finding to the Rent Controller, resolving the original isolated-span uncertainty about its author. It remains a prior adjudicative finding, not a fresh Delhi High Court determination.

source_refs.quote: The Rent Controller accepted the plea of the tenant that there was no subletting. He also accepted his plea that the requirement of the landlord for his occupation was not bona fide.

restrictions.reason: The eleven-month reasoning is explicitly attributed to both Tribunals. It is preserved as prior adjudicative reasoning about bona fides, not promoted into a universally applicable temporal legal test. Its prior-stage status does not erase the recorded finding.

source_refs.quote: It is the view of both the Tribunals that when eviction is asked for within about I I months of the letting, the claim of the landlord cannot be considered to be bonafide.

restrictions.reason: The prior finding that the landlord's occupied portion was insufficient provides limited contextual support for residential need. It does not independently determine the broader bona fide-requirement predicate or supersede the contrary prior findings. The supplied law provides no operational rule converting insufficiency into bona fides.

source_refs.quote: the portion of the premises in the occupation of the landlord was not reaso- nably sufficient

restrictions.reason: The accommodation insufficiency determination is a prior report dated May 4, 1970. The restored passage establishes the report's timing and prior character, but does not identify its author by court title within that passage. It is not converted into the target-stage High Court's independent finding. The original court-level uncertainty is retained.

source_refs.quote: held, in his report dated May 4, 1970
the portion of the premises in the occupation of the landlord was not reaso- nably sufficient

restrictions.reason: Insufficiency of the specific accommodation occupied by the landlord does not establish the absence of every other reasonably suitable residential accommodation. The finding concerns an identified occupied portion and household size; neither other possible accommodation nor a general suitability standard is supplied.

source_refs.quote: the portion of the premises in the occupation of the landlord was not reaso- nably sufficient for a family consisting of the landlord, his wife, his son, son's wife and their children.

restrictions.reason: The recorded finding directly addresses the unsuitability of the respondent's occupied premises. It does not establish that no additional reasonably suitable residential accommodation existed. The identified-accommodation finding is retained without extending it to the complete statutory negative.

source_refs.quote: the premises in the occupation of the respondent were not reasonably suitable for his residence.

restrictions.reason: The respondent named in the accommodation finding is linked to the lessor and owner through the restored factual context. The finding remains prior-stage; the supplied passage does not independently establish its author as the target High Court. Role linkage and procedural attribution are preserved separately.

source_refs.quote: The respondent who was the owner of the entire premises was then occupying the ground floor.
On this basis, he recorded a finding that the premises in the occupation of the respondent were not reasonably suitable for his residence.

restrictions.reason: No formal premises entity ID was supplied. The restored narrative nevertheless identifies the first-floor leased portion targeted by the eviction application and separately identifies the respondent's existing occupied accommodation. The absence of a database identifier is preserved as a representational limitation, not treated as proof of distinct unrelated premises or automatic failure of relational identity.

for eviction of the appellant from the portion in his occupation as lessee
was then occupying the ground floor.

restrictions.reason: The isolated original claim excerpt used 'he' without naming its antecedent. The restored parent identifies the eviction applicant as the landlord and places his asserted requirement in the same application. That contextual clarification resolves the material pronoun-attribution concern without manufacturing an entity identity from matching IDs.

that he required the premises bona fide for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

Both are retained within the same landlord-premises arrangement because they address the suitability or sufficiency of the respondent's existing occupied accommodation. They are separate evidentiary formulations, not distinct eviction transactions, and neither establishes the exhaustive absence of other accommodation.

bindings.identity_reason: The supplied narrative identifies one focal tenancy and residential-requirement dispute. The appellant leased the first floor from the respondent, the respondent owned the entire premises and occupied the ground floor, and the landlord subsequently sought eviction from the portion occupied by the appellant. The landlord's asserted residential requirement, the tenant's opposition, and the prior findings concern this same arrangement. The first-floor demised premises and the landlord's ground-floor accommodation are distinct physical objects whose relationship is established by the narrative. Neither the absence of a formal premises identifier nor disagreement about bona fides defeats this relational identity.

bindings.scope_reason: The claimed residential requirement corresponds in subject matter to the supplied clause-(e) structure. However, the independent statutory excerpt does not identify its precise enactment, territorial jurisdiction, historical version or temporal applicability to the eviction application filed in 1964. The supplied case passage identifies a Rent Controller proceeding but does not independently resolve those legal-scope details. Consequently, precise historical rule applicability remains unresolved. The earlier scope explanation improperly treated missing evidence of residential letting purpose, disputed bona fides and incomplete alternative-accommodation evidence as reasons for unresolved legal applicability. Those are substantive questions assigned respectively to C01, C02 and C06, not grounds for globally preventing the identified records from being joined.

original_identity_scope.identity_reason: The restored passages establish the respondent as lessor, owner and landlord applicant, and link the appellant's first-floor lease to the portion targeted for eviction. The respondent's ground-floor occupation and later accommodation findings are linked by the expressed party and premises relationships. No formal premises ID is supplied, but the narrative is sufficient to associate these records with one focal arrangement while preserving the distinction between leased and occupied portions.

original_identity_scope.scope_reason: The focal arrangement concerns an asserted residential requirement of identified leased premises and can be organized under the supplied clause-(e) template. The original residential letting purpose remains unstated, the exhaustive alternative-accommodation predicate is unsupported, and competing bona fide positions remain. These predicate gaps prevent treating full legal applicability and factual satisfaction as established. The independent law also does not identify its precise historical statutory version.

reviewed_join_limits.reason: The supplied historical clause-(e) wording lacks an independently identified statutory version and territorial scope. Its exact applicability to the 1964 proceeding cannot be conclusively verified from the allowed excerpts. This qualification concerns use of the proposed legal predicates, not the identity of the landlord, tenant or premises. The case evidence can remain associated with the established focal arrangement while the historical legal-scope question remains open.

reviewed_join_limits.reason: The earlier bona fide findings and accommodation findings concern the identified landlord and premises, so their prior adjudicative status does not prevent their association with the focal arrangement. Their use remains limited to accurately attributed prior findings. The eleven-month reasoning is not independently established as a general legal test, and the accommodation report is not a target-stage determination. The original proposition-specific restrictions and contrary accounts remain operative.

bindings.dependency_review_reason: The original ESTABLISHED identity assessment is retained. The original UNRESOLVED scope assessment is retained only on the narrower ground of unverified historical statutory applicability. Uncertainty about the residential purpose of the letting, competing bona fide accounts, dependency and the exhaustive absence of alternative accommodation remains within the corresponding substantive tests and existing restrictions. Prior findings remain available for review without becoming target-stage findings. No new global factual join prohibition is justified, and none of the original links, objects or restrictions is removed.

coverage_limits: All 27 original limitations are mapped to the single focal binding; no old limitation is discarded.
All six DRC_BONA_FIDE template tests are represented, including the empty C05 link list.
The landlord's separate allegation of subletting in the restored petition is not reorganized into a new clause-(e) binding because no legacy clause-(e) test link addresses that separate ground.
The first-floor leased premises and the respondent's occupied ground-floor accommodation are not treated as the same physical portion.
A missing formal premises identifier is not by itself substantive identity evidence against the coherent source-described arrangement.
The landlord-self route is distinguished from the dependent-family-member route; dependency is not inferred.

Prior findings remain prior findings. The restored Rent Controller attribution resolves one original court-level uncertainty, while the precise level of the May 1970 accommodation report remains unestablished by its supplied passage.
The absence of exhaustive accommodation evidence is limited to C06 and does not nullify the ownership or landlord-self evidence.
The supplied law contains no operational definition of bona fides, dependency or reasonable suitability, and no burden or proof-standard rule.
No final Delhi High Court determination or prediction of the clause-(e) outcome is supplied.
